title: Leaving school and learning Dixieland at the Fern
summary: He quits high school for music, meets the Dixieland players at the Fern, and learns the tunes as they call out chords.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Right. Did all this extracurricular activity bump into your schooling and did you have to quit

or did you carry on? Well, that's right. I gave up. I was going to Warren Eastern High School at the time and found out that I couldn't quite make it. So I said, well, I knew right then and there, I said, there's only one thing for me, that's music. I had no desire to learn anything else but just to play music. Now you asked me about some musicians. Here was a place where I began meeting the old Real Dixieland musicians. For instance, we had a drummer playing there by the name, he replaced the fellow that really got me the job, was Von Gammon.

Von Gammon then became leader and they had, let's see, they had Harry Shields, who was a brother of Larry Shields playing in the band. And we had an old banjo player by the name of Buzzy Willards, who was very good, and a trumpet player by the name of Bill Gillum, and a clarinet player by the name of Bill Bourgeois. Well, of course, Bill is still active today.

Right. I said, I said, Harry Shields was playing clarinet. Bill replaced Harry later on. That's right. Now, the point is this, Charlie, that in this place, all the musicians used to drop in, you see, because it was a meeting place. Shawky used to stop in there. Fasola. Fasola was about, well, when I was playing there, Fasola was a little younger than me. And you talk about something funny. He used to come around in short pants. And he weighed about, he weighed about 200 pounds with short pants and a cap. There must have been a picture. A picture is right. And he played just as wonderful then as he did later on. And, um, and...
I'm sorry, before you go on, did you mention the name of this place?
The Fern. The Fern. It was called The Fern Dance Hall. And it was on Canal Street? It was on, uh, it was on Iverville one time, and then it was also on Burgundy at one time.
Okay, thank you. Okay, now, did you want to comment any further on this is how you got into the, the...

This was the real beginning of jazz for me, as far as really jazz was concerned, because I'll never forget, I went there with a couple of pieces of music, you know, that I'd had. When I got there, Von Gammon, the leader of the band, says, what are you doing with that, homin? I said, well, I thought I might need it. He says, just take one look around. He says, do you think you'd be able to see it? I says, no, I don't think so. So Harry Shields told me, he says, don't worry, he says, I'll call the chords out to you, you know. And this is the way I learned all the Dixieland tunes, Charlie, because they'd call out jazz me blues, and I'd say, well, I don't know that. I never played it before in my life. They said, don't worry about it, we'll call the chords out to you, you see. So after about two or three nights, you'd get familiar with the tune, you know. Right. Or they'd play That's A Plenty, or jazz band ball, or Millen Boyd Joy. Is that a, the big thing in those days was a four-minute slow drag, you know. Everybody got a dime ticket or a nickel ticket. I just don't remember what they used to charge them. And this was a big dance for the fellas that would come in, because they'd give them a four-minute dance for one ticket, you see. And they'd say, the next dance is going to be a four-minute slow drag. And usually they'd play tin rule blues, which was a real good blues. And of course, this is the way that I practically learned all of the Dixieland tunes, right, right in that Fern dance hall.
